1.pericope_label: In thee, O Lord, do I put my trust; let me never be ashamed... Into thine hand I commit my spirit: thou hast redeemed me, O Lord God of truth

schools.summary: Divided between text and history. One line renders the plea literally — let me not for ever be ashamed, a rock of a stronghold, a cliff fortress where the noun changes — puts the verbs of leading and rescue in the future, and grants that praying for protection and then asserting confidence is the logic of the heart rather than the intellect. The other weighs the case for Jeremiah's authorship on the strength of shared language and plaintive tone, then refuses to let resemblance settle it, since that prophet's speech is itself steeped in the Psalter.

Insists on the tense of the opening profession — not I have trusted nor I will trust, but I do, a continued act directed to no creature — and observes that nothing but faith is brought forward, deliverance promised only because safety is believed to depend on God's power. Reads the following clause two ways: cast me not off for ever, distress for a time set against lasting confusion; or, whatever befalls, be ready to stretch out thy hand as the case requires. Takes the committed spirit of life entrusted to a faithful Creator, of the soul's eternal safety, or of a man expecting death.

Denies that the psalm can be dated or attributed with certainty, reporting the Jeremiah proposal without adopting it. Makes the stooping ear concrete — put thy ear to my lips, as with the dying — and traces the fifth verse's long service as a deathbed formula, said by the sick while they could speak and by the priest when they could not, kept in Latin inside English prayers as though the tongue were sovereign. A second voice in this school keeps the committed spirit practical: preservation asked on the strength of past rescue.

Pairs the petitions with the doctrine that faith and prayer go together, and orders them: deliverance in righteousness as well as mercy, deliverance speedily lest deferred rescue exhaust the faith that waits, shelter within the trouble if not out of it, and guidance governing conscience and prudence at once. Treats the opening avowal as a sheet anchor cast out in the storm, put first lest trial drive it from mind, and argues that it would dishonour God if faith went unrewarded.

Reads the title rather than the occasion. The word added there signifies a transport of mind produced by panic or revelation, and this psalm shows chiefly the panic of God's people under persecution. The speakers are then distinguished — the Mediator first, the redeemed people giving thanks next, the prophet interposed twice at the close.

debates.question: Who wrote the psalm, and when?

positions.summary: Undeterminable: it carries no notes of time or place, and the Jeremiah proposal rests only on shared wording.
David's, and the Jeremiah parallels prove nothing, since that prophet's language is saturated with the Psalter and may be borrowing rather than lending.
David's, plausibly after the escape from the wilderness of Maon, though the conjecture is admitted to be doubtful.

debates.question: Is the committed spirit a dying man's surrender or a living man's deposit?

positions.summary: It reaches to death: the words fit a man expecting to die, and cover the soul's eternal safety.
Death was not in the psalmist's thought at all; it was in life, amid trouble, that he deposited his spirit with God as a trust.
Neither: the spirit is committed for preservation from enemies, on the strength of past rescue.

outliers.reading: Takes the psalm's superscription as its interpretive key, assigning its parts to distinct speakers — Mediator, redeemed people, prophet — and reading the word for ecstasy as the panic of a persecuted church.

themes: In thee, O Lord, do I put my trust; let me never be ashamed: deliver me in thy righteousness.
Bow down thine ear to me; deliver me speedily: be thou my strong rock, for an house of defence to save me.
For thou art my rock and my fortress; therefore for thy name’s sake lead me, and guide me.
Pull me out of the net that they have laid privily for me: for thou art my strength.
Into thine hand I commit my spirit: thou hast redeemed me, O Lord God of truth.

6.pericope_label: I have hated them that regard lying vanities: but I trust in the Lord... I have heard the slander of many: fear was on every side

schools.summary: Works the wording of the complaint. The vanities are literally a breath of lies and undoubtedly idols; the failing strength is better read as the suffering that follows sin than as the sin itself, the Greek and Latin having poverty; belly is better body, since mind and body suffered together; the adverb rendered especially is out of place and is better a noun meaning burden, with the watchers fluttering away like frightened birds. The stretch closes with a proposal that the famous phrase means conspiracy rather than terror, and the slander a whisper.

Widens the hated vanities to the whole field of false religion and false pleasure — divination, will-worship, error, and finally all worldly enjoyment as vanity and vexation. On the reproach it observes that the thing is as it is made: under divine support the saints count it great riches, at other times it seizes their spirits. Allows that being forgotten as a dead man may mean forgotten by God, and calls that the weakness of the psalmist's faith rather than the truth of his case.

Supplies the physiology and the sociology. Grief spoils digestion, impairs the nerves and hastens death; the bowels are named as the tender part and the seat of compassion; and the word for sighing is a natural sound rather than a coined one, the noise a distressed mind makes in any language. The reproach is reconstructed as social ruin — proscribed at court, thought dangerous by neighbours, shunned as though contagious — with a second voice adding that they kept away to prevent their own danger.

Marks the change of plea from righteousness to mercy, the argument being simply the greatness of the misery, and reads the ruined health as evidence against temperament: a man ruddy and sanguine, musical and daring, has nonetheless wept out his eyes. Draws the warning that the airy and gay should take heed of extremes, since God can make them melancholy if they will not otherwise learn to be serious. On the thanksgiving it insists that praise never hinders prayer but refreshes it, and that misery moves mercy without further argument.

debates.question: What are the lying vanities the psalmist hates?

positions.summary: Idols, and specifically so — the phrase is a fixed term for them.
Idols or divination, either being admissible.
The whole class of false objects: divination, unauthorised worship, error and heresy, and finally all worldly enjoyment.

debates.question: Why does the psalmist's strength fail?

positions.summary: Because of his own sin, owned as desert — against Saul he could plead innocence, but under God's hand he confesses he deserved it.
Because of the suffering that follows sin rather than the sin itself, a sense that suits the context better; the Greek and Latin read poverty.

outliers.reading: Argues that the Hebrew word for sighing is not a coined term but a transcription of the sound grief actually makes, near enough identical across languages, and matches it to a cry from his own country.

themes: I have hated them that regard lying vanities: but I trust in the Lord.
I will be glad and rejoice in thy mercy: for thou hast considered my trouble; thou hast known my soul in adversities;
And hast not shut me up into the hand of the enemy: thou hast set my feet in a large room.
Have mercy upon me, O Lord, for I am in trouble: mine eye is consumed with grief, yea, my soul and my belly.
For my life is spent with grief, and my years with sighing: my strength faileth because of mine iniquity, and my bones are consumed.
I was a reproach among all mine enemies, but especially among my neighbours, and a fear to mine acquaintance: they that did see me without fled from me.
I am forgotten as a dead man out of mind: I am like a broken vessel.
For I have heard the slander of many: fear was on every side: while they took counsel together against me, they devised to take away my life.

14.pericope_label: But I trusted in thee, O Lord: I said, Thou art my God. My times are in thy hand... Oh how great is thy goodness, which thou hast laid up for them that fear thee

schools.summary: Calls the opening pronoun emphatic, set against the pretended panic and the real dangers alike, and widens my times to the vicissitudes of human life — destinies in the Greek and Latin — so that no machination can prevail against one whom God means to deliver; the security of the phrase is set against another idiom in which a man's soul is continually in his own hand. Hears the priestly blessing echoed in the shining face, distinguishes the word for silencing from the previous verse, prefers arrogant to grievous, and reads the treasured goodness as hidden and now displayed. A second voice grants that God appears to have given the sufferer up in anger, and that he confides even so, with the prayer of appropriating faith.

Takes my times against the enemies directly: the hour of life and death was fixed by God and no enemy could reach it early, and since prosperity and adversity alike are at his disposal the thought is a quieting one. Sees faith reviving under discouraging views, fills out the petition for a shining face with the manifestations of God's love, and identifies the lying lips with the courtiers who told Saul that David sought his throne.

Reads the confession as a settlement — thou hast been my helper hitherto, and I have taken thee for my portion — renders the plea for salvation literally as save me in thy mercy, and asks only that the slanderers' pride be abated and their devices confounded. On the closing verse it attaches the phrase about the sons of men to the trusting rather than to the display, making it the boldness of open confession amid a crooked generation, and insists the store is infinite: enough for all, for each, for evermore.

Takes the section as a renewal of the earlier petitions, as earnest wrestlers try the same hold again and again, with faith as a shield whose holding settles the issue of the battle. Divides the closing goodness in two — laid up as an inheritance reserved, wrought as goodness performed here, enough in bank and enough in hand — and lays the fault at the door of unbelief when what is laid up is not wrought for us. On the exclamation it observes that holy amazement uses interjections where adjectives fail.

debates.question: What does my times are in thy hand mean?

positions.summary: The specific hours of this man's life and death, fixed by God so that no enemy can reach him early.
The vicissitudes of human life generally — destinies, in the old versions — under divine control.

debates.question: Do the two verbs of the closing verse describe two goods or one?

positions.summary: Two: a goodness laid up as reserved inheritance and a goodness wrought out in performance, the second conditional on faith taking hold of the first.
One: a treasure hidden and then brought out and displayed, the favour not always manifested but drawn out when needed.

outliers.reading: Concedes the appearance against faith — that God has given the sufferer up in anger and made him an offscouring of all people — and calls the trust exercised in spite of that appearance a prayer of appropriating faith.

themes: But I trusted in thee, O Lord: I said, Thou art my God.
My times are in thy hand: deliver me from the hand of mine enemies, and from them that persecute me.
Make thy face to shine upon thy servant: save me for thy mercies’ sake.
Let me not be ashamed, O Lord; for I have called upon thee: let the wicked be ashamed, and let them be silent in the grave.
Let the lying lips be put to silence; which speak grievous things proudly and contemptuously against the righteous.
Oh how great is thy goodness, which thou hast laid up for them that fear thee; which thou hast wrought for them that trust in thee before the sons of men!

20.pericope_label: Thou shalt hide them in the secret of thy presence from the pride of man... Be of good courage, and he shall strengthen your heart, all ye that hope in the Lord

schools.summary: Prefers the hiding-place of thy countenance, one of several such images in the Psalms, and challenges the received sense of what the hidden are hidden from: the parallelism and the Greek favour rough or wrangling talk over arrogance, and one lexicographer renders the word conspiracies. Declines to locate the strong city at all, taking it as a general image of divine protection, reads the verb as making the kindness manifest, renders the haste literally as fleeing away in fear while noting the ancient versions' in my confusion, and suggests that preserving the faithful may be better rendered as keeping faith.

Keeps the haste literal, referring it to the flight from Saul, and ends the psalm where the psalm does — the distressed may take heart, their case being no worse than the psalmist's, and he was delivered.

Argues the strong city is Ziklag rather than Keilah, since at Keilah the walls proved no refuge, while allowing that the phrase may mean only that God's protection made him as safe as if walled in. Reads the haste inwardly, as a failure to advert to the promise under pressure of numbers. Restricts the command to love to those who can obey it, defines the faithful by the fruits of love, and turns on the proud doer with unusual heat. A second voice in this school offers three senses of the hiding place — presence chamber, tabernacle, or a secret favour saving by unknown methods — and names Keilah without hesitation.

Names the danger the hiding place answers: pride trampling and contentious men quarrelling, so that pride endangers liberty and perverse disputing endangers truth. Keeps both candidate cities and adds that God preserved the fugitive in caves and woods as safely as in either. Treats the confession of haste as a record kept against the psalmist himself, with the maxim that what is spoken amiss in haste must be repented of at leisure. On the closing exhortation it calls love towards a smiting God a work of grace, and answers fear with the promise that strengthening puts power into the fountain of vitality.

debates.question: What is the strong city in which the kindness was shown?

positions.summary: Ziklag, the fortified town given to David by the king of Gath; Keilah is excluded, its walls having been no refuge.
Keilah, where the preservation was doubly remarkable.
No city at all: a general image of divine protection, or at most the claim that God's care made him as safe as if walled in.

debates.question: Was the psalmist's rash word spoken in flight or in confusion of mind?

positions.summary: In literal flight — the phrase renders as my fleeing away in fear.
In inward confusion: passion displaced consideration, weakened faith, and produced a conclusion drawn from the number of his enemies.

outliers.reading: Abandons exposition at the mention of the proud doer for a direct denunciation, asking what a sinner and heir of wretchedness can possibly be proud of, and promising such men their due and nothing but their due.

themes: Thou shalt hide them in the secret of thy presence from the pride of man: thou shalt keep them secretly in a pavilion from the strife of tongues.
Blessed be the Lord: for he hath shewed me his marvellous kindness in a strong city.
For I said in my haste, I am cut off from before thine eyes: nevertheless thou heardest the voice of my supplications when I cried unto thee.
O love the Lord, all ye his saints: for the Lord preserveth the faithful, and plentifully rewardeth the proud doer.
Be of good courage, and he shall strengthen your heart, all ye that hope in the Lord.
